history.contentIn: The Paris Agreement is a legally binding international treaty on climate change adopted by 196 Parties at COP21 in Paris on 12 December 2015 and in force from 4 November 2016. Its central aim is to hold the increase in the global average temperature to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels and to pursue efforts to limit the increase to 1.5°C. Parties submit nationally determined contributions (NDCs) describing their mitigation plans; the Agreement uses a ratchet mechanism of successive NDCs rather than a single top-down allocation of tonnes. The treaty does not ban talking about geoengineering, but it is not a secret authorisation to spray the atmosphere. Article 4 addresses peaking of greenhouse gas emissions and a balance between anthropogenic emissions by sources and removals by sinks in the second half of the century (often discussed as net-zero CO2). The United States joined, withdrew under the first Trump administration, and rejoined under the Biden administration; participation has been politically contested but the scientific case for rapid emissions cuts is independent of any one administration. Meeting Paris temperature goals requires deep, sustained cuts in fossil CO2, methane and other greenhouse gases, plus protection of carbon sinks — not covert aviation spraying.
